query: Our UniFi network spans 14 sites across three regional offices, and over the past year different team members have created separate markdown files documenting host inventories, device configs, VLAN assignments, and troubleshooting runbooks — but there's massive overlap and contradiction between them. I need you to first pull a current inventory of all hosts and devices across every UniFi site so we have an accurate baseline of what's actually deployed (include status, model, firmware, IP, and which site each belongs to), then take the 23 documentation files in our `/docs/infrastructure/` folder and consolidate them into a clean, non-redundant set. Merge the VLAN docs (there are four covering nearly the same content), combine the three overlapping troubleshooting guides, and unify the per-site inventory docs into one canonical source-of-truth document that reflects the live infrastructure data you just pulled. Make sure nothing valuable gets lost — some files have unique notes about firmware quirks or site-specific firewall rules that only appear once — but eliminate all the duplicated and outdated content.

Our team just refactored the markdown rendering pipeline in our `docs-engine` repo and I noticed the PR description template we use has several broken relative links — things like `[Architecture Guide](docs/architecture.md)` and `[Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md)` that don't resolve properly on GitHub when people view the PR. I also want to update the `src/renderer/markdownParser.ts` file to handle GFM autolinks and reference-style links correctly, since right now it silently drops them. Can you validate and fix all the markdown links in our PR description template at `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` so they point to proper blob URLs on the `main` branch, and then propose the code changes needed in `markdownParser.ts` to support those link types? Show me the diffs and your reasoning for each change before anything gets merged.

We have a Python SDK called `atlas-geo` for geospatial tile rendering that we're about to open-source. The package has about 30 public modules across `atlas_geo.layers`, `atlas_geo.projections`, `atlas_geo.tiles`, and `atlas_geo.styles` namespaces — all classes and functions already have Google-style docstrings with Args, Returns, Raises, and Examples sections. Can you generate a complete API reference in Markdown from those docstrings? I want one `.md` file per subpackage with a table of contents, all public classes and their methods documented with parameter types and descriptions, cross-links between related classes (e.g., `TileRenderer` references `Projection`), and a top-level `index.md` that gives an overview of the package architecture. Please also include usage examples pulled from the docstring `Examples` blocks formatted as fenced code blocks, and flag any public symbols that are missing docstrings so we can fix them before release.

We have an epic in our Jira backlog called "Veterinary Clinic Patient Portal" that covers everything from pet owners booking appointments online, viewing vaccination records, receiving medication reminders, messaging their vet, and paying invoices. The team estimated it at around 80 story points and it's way too large to pull into a sprint. Can you break this epic down into well-defined user stories with acceptance criteria for each? Please make sure each story is small enough to complete in a single sprint, follows the INVEST principles, and is written from the perspective of the appropriate persona (pet owner, veterinarian, or clinic receptionist). If any story still feels too big after the initial split, break it down further.

I'm a mid-level backend developer (2 years Python, basic SQL, no cloud experience) who wants to transition into a cloud/DevOps engineering role within 18 months while keeping my current job. Can you design a detailed learning roadmap for me — but I want you to approach it by first mapping out all the common ways people fail at this transition (burning out from too many certs at once, learning tools without understanding networking fundamentals, skipping hands-on projects, neglecting the cultural/process side of DevOps, etc.), and then structure the plan specifically to avoid each of those failure modes? For each phase of the plan, explicitly call out which failure pattern it's designed to prevent, what the warning signs of that failure look like so I can self-diagnose, and what corrective action to take if I notice myself slipping. I'd also like the plan to account for the fact that I only have about 8-10 hours per week to dedicate to learning.

We just merged a PR into our "StreamDeck" event-driven analytics service (TypeScript, Node 20) that ingests webhook payloads from Stripe, GitHub, and Slack. The problem is the incoming `event` objects are typed as `unknown` and we've been unsafely casting them with `as StripeEvent` etc., which caused a prod bug last night — a malformed GitHub webhook with a missing `action` field slipped through and crashed the handler. I need two things: first, refactor the event ingestion layer to use proper custom type guard functions (e.g., `function isStripeEvent(payload: unknown): payload is StripeEvent`) that validate the shape of each webhook payload at runtime before routing, including nested discriminated unions for sub-event types like `checkout.session.completed` vs `invoice.payment_failed`. Second, since this was a production bug and we're also adding new behavior with these guards, update our living docs — log the webhook crash bug and its fix in the team guide's bug list, add a dev changelog entry describing the type guard refactor, note an idea I had about eventually generating these guards automatically from each provider's OpenAPI spec in the ideas doc, and add a task for next session to write integration tests that send malformed payloads against all the new guards.

Our marketing team just finished a new set of promotional banners, social media templates, and localized landing page mockups for our "Pinnacle Gear" outdoor apparel brand launch across EN, FR, DE, and JA markets. I need two things done: First, I want to automate publishing these assets to our GitHub repo (`pinnacle-gear/campaign-assets`) with proper release tags using the `gh` CLI, but when I try running `gh auth login` on our new CI runner (Ubuntu 24.04), I get a "command not found" error, and on my Mac I'm getting a 401 when trying to push a release — can you walk me through getting `gh` properly installed and authenticated on both environments so we can script the release? Second, before we push anything, I need you to help me build a QA checklist we can run against all the creative assets — specifically checking that every banner and template follows our brand guidelines (correct Pinnacle Gear logo placement, approved color palette #1B3A4B / #F5A623 / #FFFFFF), meets WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards for contrast and alt text, and that all localized versions have correct translations, proper date/number formatting per locale, and no truncated text in the FR/DE/JA variants. Can you give me the full setup walkthrough and then the checklist?

We're building "RSSVibe," a Swift/SwiftUI RSS reader app targeting international markets. I need two things done together: First, design a RESTful API hierarchy for our backend — we need endpoints for managing feeds, articles, categories, and user preferences, using TypedResults for consistent response typing, with proper documentation comments and versioned paths. Second, for the SwiftUI client consuming this API, all user-facing strings (error messages from API responses, feed category names, empty state descriptions, button labels, etc.) need to be fully localized using `LocalizedStringResource` and `.xcstrings` String Catalogs instead of the old `Localizable.strings` approach. I want type-safe localization keys organized by feature module so our translators can work independently. Can you sketch out the API endpoint design with sample TypedResults return types, and then show the corresponding Swift client layer where every UI string — including dynamically constructed ones like "You have \(count) unread articles in \(feedName)" — uses the new String Catalog workflow with proper pluralization rules and interpolation?

Set up a reusable component library for our internal project management tool "TaskForge" using Next.js and Tailwind CSS with shadcn/ui as the foundation. We need a custom design token system with our brand colors (primary: #1E40AF, secondary: #9333EA, surface: #F8FAFC, destructive: #DC2626), consistent spacing scale, and typography tokens that map to Tailwind's config. Build out these components: 1) A `KanbanCard` component with priority badges (P0-P3) that use color-coded tokens, assignee avatars, due date chips, and subtle hover/focus ring states for accessibility — it needs to look good at both compact and expanded sizes. 2) A `SprintSidebar` with collapsible sections, active state indicators, and keyboard navigation support. 3) A responsive `DashboardHeader` with a command palette trigger, breadcrumbs, and a notification bell with a count badge. For all components, make sure we're using CSS custom properties as design tokens that feed into `tailwind.config.ts` so we can support light/dark mode toggling without duplicating classes everywhere. Also include proper `aria-` attributes, focus-visible rings using our token system, and ensure the color contrast ratios meet WCAG AA. Show me the tailwind config, the CSS token layer, and the three components.

We're about to split our monorepo project "ClimateLens" (a climate data visualization platform) into two independently deployable services — a Rust ingestion pipeline and a Python/FastAPI analytics API — and we want to manage this transition using SpecWeave. Right now everything lives under a single `spec.md` and `tasks.md`, but after the split each service will have its own release cadence, its own set of living docs, and potentially divergent API contracts that downstream dashboard consumers depend on. I need help designing the increment structure and naming conventions so that cross-service breaking changes (like a schema migration in the ingestion pipeline that ripples into the analytics API's query layer and then into the frontend's caching assumptions) are tracked as linked increments with explicit dependency edges rather than silently drifting apart. Specifically: how should we structure the source-of-truth files and post-task-completion hooks so that completing an increment in one service automatically flags dependent increments in the other as "blocked-needs-review," and what conventions should the `tasks.md` entries follow so that a future engineer reading the history can trace the second- and third-order impacts of any given change — for example, if we change the NetCDF chunking strategy in ingestion, it affects not just the analytics query performance but also the CDN cache hit rates for the public tile server two hops downstream?

I've been writing a screenplay in Fountain format using VS Code with the Better Fountain extension, and now my producer needs delivery files. Can you walk me through exporting it to both a properly formatted PDF and a Final Draft .fdx file? I'd also like to generate an HTML preview I can share with the director via a link. I'm open to using afterwriting CLI or Highland — whatever gets the cleanest output. The script is called "Vanishing Tides.fountain" and lives in my project root.

I'm building a procedural underwater scene in GLSL for our indie game "AbyssVoyager" — the camera slowly descends through ocean depth zones. I need help figuring out the right approach: the shallow zone needs animated caustic light patterns on a sandy floor, the mid-depth zone should have bioluminescent jellyfish with translucent glowing bodies, and the deep trench zone needs volumetric fog with god rays filtering down. I also want smooth signed-distance-field coral formations that morph organically along the descent. Can you help me figure out which shader techniques I should combine for each zone and map out an overall architecture for the fragment shader pipeline?

We're building "ChronoArena," a fully onchain turn-based strategy game on Starknet using the Dojo engine, and we also have a companion web app built with Next.js App Router (strict TypeScript, ShadCN UI) called "Quetrex" that serves as the game's lobby, leaderboard, and replay viewer. I need help with both sides simultaneously. On the Dojo side, I need to implement a new `BattleSystem` that handles a rock-paper-scissors combat resolution mechanic — each player submits a `CommitAction` with a hashed move, then a `RevealAction` that checks the hash and resolves damage against the opponent's `HealthComponent` and `ShieldComponent` models, with a timeout mechanism that auto-forfeits if a player doesn't reveal within 10 blocks. The system also needs to emit events that Torii can index for the frontend. On the Quetrex side, I need a new `/matches/[matchId]/replay` route that fetches the indexed battle events from our Torii GraphQL endpoint, renders them as an animated timeline using ShadCN `Card`, `Badge`, and `Tooltip` components, and lets users step through each round. This feature needs full TDD coverage — unit tests for the event-parsing utilities and integration tests for the replay page using Testing Library. Also make sure the GraphQL calls go through a server action so we don't leak the Torii endpoint to the client, and validate all incoming params with Zod. Can you walk me through the architecture for both pieces and then start with the Dojo system implementation and the corresponding Quetrex replay feature scaffolding?

Our research lab is building a sensor data acquisition framework called "AgroSense" in Pharo Smalltalk — it collects telemetry from LoRa-connected soil moisture and temperature sensors deployed across experimental farm plots, processes the readings locally on Raspberry Pi edge gateways, and publishes aggregated metrics via MQTT. I need help structuring the Tonel package layout for this. Specifically, I want a `BaselineOf` that declares dependencies between our packages: `AgroSense-Core` (domain models for sensor readings, device registries), `AgroSense-MQTT` (an MQTT 3.1.1 client wrapper handling QoS levels and last-will messages for intermittent connectivity), `AgroSense-EdgePipeline` (a local aggregation pipeline that downsamples raw 1Hz ADC readings into 5-minute averages to conserve bandwidth on our LoRaWAN backhaul), and `AgroSense-Tests`. Can you give me the full Tonel `.st` files for the key classes? For the `SoilMoistureSensor` class I need instance variables tracking the device EUI, calibration coefficients, and a ring buffer for raw readings, plus a method category `'mqtt-serialization'` with a method that encodes a CBOR-like compact payload (we're limited to 51-byte LoRa frames at SF12). Also include the `EdgeAggregator` class that implements a sliding window average with configurable window size and handles out-of-order packet arrival using sequence numbers — this matters because our LoRa gateway sometimes receives retransmitted frames. Show proper CRC-style class comments, the `package.st` files, and the correct directory tree structure. I keep getting import failures when I load the packages in Pharo 12 because the `BaselineOf` tries to load `AgroSense-MQTT` before `AgroSense-Core` — what's the right way to declare the dependency ordering?

We have a microservices platform called "TideWatch" — it's an ocean monitoring system with six Rust services behind an Envoy gateway, all deployed via Helm charts to a GKE cluster. Two things I need help with: First, I want to set up an automated canary deployment pipeline using Argo Rollouts for our `wave-analyzer` service — it should gradually shift traffic from the stable version to the canary (10% → 25% → 50% → 100%) with automated metric analysis gates pulling from our Prometheus instance, and automatic rollback if p99 latency exceeds 200ms or error rate goes above 1%. I need the full AnalysisTemplate, Rollout manifest, and the GitHub Actions workflow that triggers it on merge to main. Second, the `wave-analyzer` service itself needs optimization — it's doing FFT on streaming hydrophone data and the current implementation is CPU-bound. The core transform loop processes 2048-sample windows and I think we can parallelize it with Rayon, but I also want to evaluate whether this is a task worth throwing heavy compute at or if a lighter model would suffice. Given the complexity difference between these two asks — one is mostly YAML wiring and CI config, the other involves algorithmic optimization in Rust — which Claude model tier would you recommend I use for each part to balance cost and quality? And for the deployment piece, what other release strategies or tooling should I be considering beyond Argo Rollouts for our stack?

Can you write me a 45-second script for a TikTok Reel promoting my new Python-based SaaS tool "CalorieLens" (an AI food scanner app)? I need a killer hook in the first 1.5 seconds, a pattern interrupt around second 8, and a CTA at the end — but please make sure the script doesn't sound like generic AI slop. Write it in a conversational, slightly sarcastic voice like I'm talking to a friend, use specific numbers and concrete visuals instead of vague hype, and structure it with exact timestamps and on-screen text cues so my editor can cut it. Also include notes on pacing, where to add jump cuts for retention, and a suggested trending audio style. I want this thing to hit 90%+ watch-through rate.

Our startup "ChartWell" is a health analytics platform and we just kicked off a new session in this repo. Before we start coding, scan the monorepo structure (`packages/ingestion`, `packages/dashboard`, `apps/api`, `apps/web`, `libs/shared-types`) and register everything in the project metadata file so our tooling stays current. Also, while you're in there — the `apps/api` package has a `/v1/patient-notes` endpoint that accepts freeform clinician text and stores it. I'm worried that users (or prompt-injection attempts) could feed it text containing explicit self-harm instructions, graphic violence, or other harmful content that then gets surfaced verbatim in the dashboard summaries. Add a middleware content-screening layer before persistence that detects and rejects messages containing dangerous content categories (detailed instructions for self-harm, CSAM references, doxxing PII patterns, etc.), returns an appropriate 422 response with a safe error message, and logs the event without echoing back the offending content. Give me the middleware implementation in TypeScript and the updated route wiring, plus confirm the metadata registry has been refreshed with the current project topology.

Our team just wrapped up a sprint planning session for "DiscoHy," our Python-based distributed topology computation library that uses thread operads. I recorded the whole meeting and need three things done: First, set up the project scaffolding using `uv` for dependency management with `ruff` for linting, making sure the `pyproject.toml` has the right configuration for our DiscoHy Thread Operad modules and that `uvx` can run our test suite. Second, take these raw meeting notes from today's planning session and structure them properly — extract all the action items, assign owners, note the decisions we made about the new homology computation API, and flag the governance items about our open-source licensing vote that need to go to the steering committee. Third, our GitHub Actions CI pipeline is painfully slow (18+ minutes) mainly because `uv pip install` and `ruff` checks re-download and re-process everything from scratch on each run — design a caching strategy for the `uv` dependency cache, ruff's cache directory, and our operad computation test fixtures, and show me before/after estimated build times. Here are the raw notes from the meeting: "Standup 2025-06-18: attendees: @maria, @josh, @priya, @devon. Discussed migrating from setup.py to uv-managed pyproject.toml. Josh volunteers to handle ruff rule configuration for the operad module. Priya raised concern about CI taking too long — agreed to investigate pipeline caching. Decision: adopt MIT license pending steering committee approval by June 25. Devon to benchmark thread operad test suite..."

I'm working on a dynamical systems homework problem and struggling with the analysis. Consider the ODE dx/dt = r + x² where r is a real parameter. I need to find the critical value of r where equilibria appear or disappear, sketch the bifurcation diagram in the (r, x) plane showing the stable and unstable branches, determine the stability of each equilibrium on either side of the critical parameter value, and explain physically what happens to the system's long-term behavior as r slowly increases through the critical point. Also, can you write a Python script using matplotlib that numerically integrates this system for several values of r near the bifurcation point and animates the phase portraits to visualize how the two fixed points collide and annihilate each other?

We're redesigning our B2B fintech dashboard app "ClearLedger" and I need help developing the initial UI concept direction. Here's what we know from user research: our users are primarily CFOs and accounting managers who feel overwhelmed by data density, want faster access to cash flow forecasts, and frequently switch between reconciliation and reporting views. The brand guidelines call for "confident calm" — think muted blues with sharp typographic hierarchy. Based on these insights, can you create a detailed conceptual design exploration that includes: (1) a mood board describing the visual language — color palettes, type pairings, spatial rhythm, and reference interfaces that capture the "confident calm" feel, (2) two contrasting UI concept directions for the main dashboard view (one that prioritizes progressive disclosure with a card-based layout, another that uses a dense data-table approach with contextual sidebars), with annotated wireframe descriptions explaining the strategic rationale behind each layout choice, and (3) an interaction concept for the cash flow forecast widget showing how hover states, drill-downs, and time-range selections would behave — described well enough that I could build an interactive Figma prototype from it. For each concept direction, explain how it maps back to the specific research findings and what kind of user feedback each is designed to provoke when we test them.

Our production Kubernetes cluster is running a data ingestion pipeline called "TideStream" and something's gone haywire — one of the worker pods keeps spawning runaway Python processes that are eating all the CPU on node `ingest-07`. I need you to SSH into that node, list all processes sorted by CPU usage to identify the culprits, find any zombie or orphaned processes related to our `tidestream-worker` service, and kill them gracefully (SIGTERM first, then SIGKILL if they don't die within 10 seconds). Also, we have a tmux session called `ingest-monitor` on that box that one of our SREs left running last week — can you check if it's still alive, list all its windows/panes to see what's in there, and if there's a pane tailing logs from the old v2.1 pipeline, kill that process and close that pane but keep the rest of the session intact? Finally, write me a bash script I can cron-schedule that monitors for any `tidestream-worker` child processes exceeding 90% CPU for more than 2 minutes and automatically kills them, logging the PID, command, and timestamp to `/var/log/tidestream-watchdog.log`.

Our Python monorepo "AstroGrid" is a distributed radio telescope data processing pipeline with 12 major modules (`ingestion`, `calibration`, `imaging`, `spectral_analysis`, `catalog`, `scheduler`, `auth`, `storage_backend`, `monitoring`, `alerting`, `web_dashboard`, `plugin_sdk`). We recently onboarded three new team members and realized we have almost zero project-level documentation — people keep asking the same questions about module boundaries, shared conventions, data flow between pipeline stages, and which config flags are experimental. I want you to create a comprehensive `CLAUDE.md` at the repo root that serves as a master index: it should describe the overall architecture, list every module with a one-line purpose and link to its own docs, cover cross-cutting concerns (error handling strategy, logging conventions, our custom `@retriable` decorator protocol, env var naming scheme), and note the critical "do not modify" invariants around the `calibration` module's FFT kernel ordering. Then create individual `CLAUDE.md` files for the four most complex modules — `calibration`, `imaging`, `spectral_analysis`, and `plugin_sdk` — each documenting their internal structure, public API surfaces, key algorithms with references to the relevant papers, configuration knobs, testing strategy, and inter-module dependencies. For `plugin_sdk` specifically, include the hook lifecycle, type contracts third-party plugins must satisfy, and the versioning/deprecation policy. Make sure everything is hierarchical and machine-readable so future AI-assisted development sessions can quickly orient themselves.

We're building a multiplayer browser game called "MedFortress" using Three.js where players construct and defend hospital compound bases — think Fortnite-style building mechanics but set in a healthcare/biotech theme. The game has destructible structures (walls, server rooms, labs) with cascading collapse when load-bearing elements are destroyed, and we need the structural integrity simulation to feel satisfying with proper damage propagation and support detection so floating pieces don't just hang in the air. Here's the twist: the game is being developed by a HealthTech company ("VitaShield") that is currently pursuing ISO 27001 certification, and the game itself collects player telemetry data, account credentials, and in some regions integrates with real patient wellness APIs for a "gamified recovery" feature. I need two things in one go: (1) help me architect the structural physics system — we want a heuristic stability model where each building piece has a support graph, damage reduces connection strength, and when a node loses all support paths to the ground the whole subgraph detaches and triggers a collapse sequence with debris; and (2) review and help me design the ISMS scope and security controls specifically for this project, since our compliance consultant says the patient wellness API integration and telemetry collection put us squarely in HealthTech territory for ISO 27001 Annex A controls, and we need to map out which controls from ISO 27002:2022 apply to the game backend, how to handle the risk assessment for the wellness data flows, and what our Statement of Applicability should look like given that most of our infrastructure is a game server rather than a traditional clinical system. Can you tackle both the physics architecture and the ISMS/compliance design together?

Our e-commerce analytics team has raw clickstream data landing as gzipped JSON files in S3 (roughly 2TB/day across ~15,000 partitioned files), plus order transaction logs in a PostgreSQL RDS instance and product catalog updates streamed via Kafka. We need to build a unified data pipeline that joins these three sources into a cleaned, deduplicated "customer journey" dataset in our Snowflake warehouse, refreshed every 30 minutes. The tricky parts: the clickstream JSON schema drifts weekly as the frontend team ships new event types, the Kafka topic uses Avro with a schema registry that occasionally has backward-incompatible changes, and the Postgres tables have slowly changing dimensions (SCD Type 2) for product pricing. Can you design the end-to-end architecture — including ingestion, schema evolution handling, transformation/deduplication logic, orchestration (we're leaning toward Airflow but open to alternatives), and the final Snowflake table design with proper clustering keys for our most common query patterns (funnel analysis by product category and 7-day attribution windows)? Also include a strategy for backfilling historical data without disrupting the live pipeline and a monitoring/alerting approach for data quality issues like late-arriving events or schema breakage.

Our quant desk runs a Python pricing engine ("PharmaVol") that values exotic options on pharmaceutical stock baskets using Monte Carlo simulation with Heston stochastic volatility (CIR process for variance, Euler-Milstein discretization) plus Merton jump-diffusion for event risk around FDA approval dates. We're hitting two problems simultaneously. First, the simulated paths and Greeks are being served via a FastAPI endpoint that's painfully slow under load — we cache intermediate path results and vol surface interpolations in a two-layer setup (in-process LRU + Redis), but our Redis hit rate for the SDE path cache has dropped from 92% to ~60% after we increased the number of timesteps in the discretization scheme, and memory usage is spiking. I suspect the cache key strategy (hashing the full parameter vector including seed) is generating too many unique entries and we need a smarter bucketing or TTL eviction approach — maybe caching at the variance grid level rather than per-path. Second, because PharmaVol is used to price derivatives on pharma equities that fall under FDA regulatory oversight, our compliance team requires a full GAMP-5 compliant audit trail of every LLM-assisted pricing decision we make. We have Langfuse Cloud (EU region) collecting traces from the LLM calls that auto-select jump intensity parameters and mean-reversion speeds based on drug pipeline stage — I need a script that pulls all traces and observations from Langfuse for a given date range and user/session, computes cost and latency metrics per trace, and exports an ALCOA+ compliant report as a pandas DataFrame suitable for regulatory submission. Can you help me with all three pieces: (1) refactor the Monte Carlo + jump-diffusion simulation to use a more numerically stable scheme and properly handle the Feller condition violations we're seeing, (2) redesign the caching architecture so the SDE grid results are efficiently shared across similar parameter requests without blowing up Redis memory, and (3) build the Langfuse extraction and audit report pipeline?

Set up a Claude Code agent called "DocuMentor" that acts as an internal documentation reviewer for our Python monorepo — it should spawn subagents for each package directory to check docstring coverage, flag missing type hints, and suggest improvements based on Google-style docstring conventions. Give it a skill for generating weekly summary reports as Markdown. Once you've got the agent config scaffolded out, add a highlight for today noting the new DocuMentor agent launch along with a brief description of its capabilities and the three subagent roles it delegates to.

We're redesigning the onboarding flow for our "BrightPath" employee wellness web app — it's a multi-step signup wizard (choose a wellness plan, set goals, connect wearable devices, confirm). The current version is cluttered with gradients, drop shadows, and inconsistent button styles, and our latest audit flagged 14 WCAG 2.1 AA violations including missing focus indicators, insufficient color contrast on the step-progress bar, and no skip-navigation for keyboard users. I need you to propose a clean, flat redesign of the entire wizard — wireframes or detailed specs for each step, a cohesive color palette that passes AA contrast ratios for both normal and large text, proper focus management between steps, appropriate ARIA roles for the progress indicator, and touch target sizing for mobile. Also, the product manager wants the "connect wearable" step to be optional but discoverable — help me figure out the best pattern for that so users don't feel forced but also don't miss it. For each design decision, explain the tradeoff so I can present the rationale to stakeholders.

We're implementing a document approval system in our ERPNext instance for our manufacturing company "SteelCore." We need a Frappe Workflow for our custom doctype `Material Inspection Report` that handles quality control sign-offs. The flow should be: an inspector submits the report (Draft → Pending Review), then a QC Lead can either approve it (Pending Review → Approved) or reject it back (Pending Review → Rejected). If rejected, the inspector can resubmit (Rejected → Pending Review). Approved reports go to the Plant Manager for final sign-off (Approved → Final Approved) or can be sent back (Approved → Pending Review). Only Final Approved reports should trigger the `on_submit` hook. Please include the full workflow JSON with states, transitions, allowed roles, and the conditions for each transition. Also set it up so that email notifications go out at each state change, and make sure the workflow prevents deletion of any report that's past the Draft state.

We're wrapping up a sprint on "Tzurot v3," our agency's Webflow-based content platform that manages case studies, team bios, and service pages. During this sprint I was writing BDD specs for our "Related Case Studies" feature — which auto-links case studies to service pages based on shared CMS reference fields — and I hit several issues I need help sorting out. First, while implementing the test for "when a case study belongs to multiple service categories," I discovered that our Webflow CMS collection structure doesn't handle the many-to-many relationship cleanly; the multi-reference field on the Case Studies collection points to Services, but there's no inverse reference, and our tests revealed that when two case studies share the same service tag and one gets unpublished, the other's "Related" section sometimes shows a stale entry. I also found a race condition in our Webflow logic: if an editor publishes a new case study and simultaneously updates the linked service page, the CMS API webhook fires twice and our staging build occasionally renders the old reference list. So I need three things: (1) help me restructure the Webflow CMS collections to properly model this bidirectional relationship — should I use a junction collection or is there a cleaner pattern for multi-references in Webflow? (2) Based on what I've discovered in these test scenarios, help me refine the original requirements doc for the Related Case Studies feature to capture these edge cases (stale references on unpublish, concurrent publish race condition, and the rule that a case study should never appear in its own "Related" section on a service page), and (3) update our CURRENT_WORK.md and the folder structure docs to reflect the new collection architecture and these requirement changes before I close out this session.

Our QA team manages test scenarios for a community discussion platform built on Postmill (a Reddit-like forum engine). We need to automate the end-to-end testing of several user journeys — account registration, creating new forums, posting threads, editing wiki pages, and moderating content. Right now our test cases are written as Gherkin feature files, but we lack proper process documentation tying them together. Can you help me with two things? First, write the automation scripts (Python + Selenium or Playwright) that perform the full lifecycle on our staging Postmill instance at `https://staging.communityhub.internal`: create a test account, create a forum called "release-notes", post an announcement thread, and then update the forum's wiki sidebar with a welcome message. Second, generate a BPMN 2.0 XML diagram that models this entire forum onboarding workflow as a business process — each task node should reference the corresponding Gherkin scenario tag (like `@account-creation`, `@forum-setup`, `@first-post`, `@wiki-update`) so that our CI pipeline can link process steps to test coverage. Include proper sequence flows, gateways for error handling (e.g., if account creation fails due to rate limiting, retry after a delay), and make sure the BPMN is valid against the BPMN 2.0 schema.
